question.text: Twenty people were executed for being associated with the Devil during these series of hearings. Arthur Miller wrote about these events in The Crucible.
question.clue: They started after doctor William Griggs provided treatment for certain hysterical fits, and "spectral evidence" during these events was allowed by Cotton Mather.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about early colonization of the Americas.
swap.text: This was the first permanent English settlement in North America, founded in 1607. It nearly succumbed to famine in its early years, but was kept afloat by the leadership of John Smith and Lord De La Warr.
swap.clue: The first meeting of the House of Burgesses took place here, and it was burned to the ground during Bacon's Rebellion.

question.leadin: This citizen of the Massachusetts Bay Colony was tried in 1637 for "traducing," or slandering, the local ministers.
question.text: Name this 17th-century woman who was sentenced in a trial overseen by John Winthrop for holding prayer sessions for women and speaking out against religious gender norms.
question.clue: John Winthrop presided over a trial of this woman, leading Roger Williams to support her founding of Portsmouth, Rhode Island.

swap.text: While the route he took is under debate, this man was the first European to cross the Mississippi River, on whose banks he would perish due to fever.
swap.clue: After he died of illness, his mission was continued by Luis de Moscoso Alvarado.

question.text: This period of famine during the history of the Jamestown colony was relieved by a supply convoy led by Baron De La Warr. Evidence of cannibalism during this period has been discovered near the Jamestown colony.
question.clue: A major cause of this period, during which some relief came from trade with the Nansemonds, was the failure of the Third Supply due to the wreck of the Sea Venture, an event which inspired The Tempest.

swap.leadin: This common-law constitution contained 11 laws and was modelled on the Massachusetts Bay Colony's charter.
swap.text: Name this 1638 state constitution written by Roger Ludlow, which established a self-governing colony around Windsor, Wethersfield, and a modern-day state's capital.

question.leadin: Established by Charles II, this government's lieutenant governor Francis Nicholson was overthrown in Leisler's Rebellion.
question.text: Name this government, led by Edmund Andros, that attempted to unite many of the American colonies, and which was overthrown after the Glorious Revolution.
question.clue: Its first president later became chief justice of New York, and sentenced Jacob Leisler to death for treason.

swap.leadin: Name these founders of U.S. States.
swap.text: This Quaker received permission from King James II to establish a state known for its religious tolerance, nicknamed the "Keystone State."
swap.clue: In an event depicted by a Benjamin West painting, this man expanded his holdings by signing treaties with the Lenape tribe after he was given a colony by Charles II.

question.text: He replaced Willem Kieft as governor and conquered Swedish Delaware. For 15 points, identify this one-legged governor who served as the last Dutch colonial leader of New York.
question.clue: He was also plagued by poor Indian relations, as shown by the outbreak of the Peach Tree War and conflicts near the village of Esopus, which he renamed Wildwyck.

swap.text: This military officer sailed on the Mayflower to Plymouth Colony, where he led expeditions to break up a colony at Merry Mount. There isn't any evidence that he was in a love triangle with John Alden and Priscilla Mullins.
swap.clue: This leader of the Plymouth Colony militia. His unsuccessful wooing of Priscilla Mullens was fictionalized in a Henry Wadsworth Longfellow poem titled for his "courtship."

question.leadin: Name the following from the early settling of the English in America.
question.text: This man wanted to found a colony for debtors in America and eventually got a charter from George II to start the colony of Georgia.
question.clue: This man advocated for an excise tax on malt liquor to fund a comprehensive reform of the prison system of England while head of the Gaols ] Committee.

swap.text: This famous British preacher was noted for his open-air preaching and revival meetings in the United States. Franklin wrote descriptions of this man's revivals in Philadelphia.
swap.clue: Eulogized by Phyllis Wheatley, this Methodist minister preached in open air and broke with John Wesley over the doctrine of Arminianism.

question.leadin: A boy who befriended Richard Pace warned colonists of a 1622 attack by this ruler's brother, Opechancanough [oh-peh-CHAN-ka-"no"], that massacred hundreds.
question.text: Name this chief of a namesake Algonquian tribal confederation in modern-day Virginia that ruled the region of Tsenacomoco.
question.clue: He was the high chief among the weorance and held the title of mamanatowick or "emperor" from his capital of Werowocomoco.

swap.text: As an apprentice, Benjamin Franklin printed the New-England Courant newspaper, which featured this female persona of his giving humorous accounts of colonial life.
swap.clue: Benjamin Franklin, who wrote Poor Richard's Almanack, had earlier written in the New England Courant under this pseudonym. 14 letters published in 1722 were attributed to Franklin under this pseudonym.

question.leadin: This ethnic group drew from the native and colonized populations of the Plantation of Ulster.
question.text: Name this primarily Presbyterian ethnic group which settled in the backcountry stretching from Pennsylvania to Georgia.

swap.leadin: Lieutenant Governor William Bull opposed this event, which was led by a man named Jemmy, or Cato, along a namesake river.
swap.text: Name this 1739 slave revolt in South Carolina, the largest in the Southern colonies, whose leaders were from the Kingdom of Kongo. It led to the passage of the Negro Act of 1740.
swap.clue: During this event, participants marched toward Spanish Florida from South Carolina carrying a banner that read "Liberty!"

question.leadin: Jeremiah Gridley argued for the legality of these instruments, which were introduced to enforce the Acts of Trade, and his argument was upheld by Chief Justice Thomas Hutchinson.
question.text: Name these general search warrants, which gave customs officers legal authority to inspect ships and homes at will, and were thus quite controversial in colonial America.

swap.leadin: This collection includes "What is an American?" and "Distresses of a Frontier Man." It was written at the author's Hudson River plantation Pine Hill.
swap.text: Name this set of 12 letters, published in 1782, which uses a fictional narrator James to describe local American customs and life on the frontier.
swap.clue: The third one claims that in the United States, "individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men," and is titled "What is an American?"

question.text: The revolt was crushed at this two-hour battle, where the Regulators told Tryon to "fire and be damned" after being told to lay down their arms.

swap.leadin: Answer questions about the early history of North Carolina.
swap.text: This Native American tribe fought a namesake war in 1711 with British colonists under leadership of Chiefs Tom Blunt and Hancock, who turned on each other in some classic Indian-on-Indian violence. After being defeated, this tribe migrated north to become the sixth Iroquois nation.
swap.clue: They threatened to take sides in the struggle between Thomas Cary and Governor Hyde, and ultimately formed alliances with the Nynee and Bear River peoples to prosecute an unsuccessful 1711 to 1713 war against North Carolina.
